articles.title: DeafCity Hub and the fight to build a space where sign language can live and thrive
articles.summary:

The post DeafCity Hub and the fight to build a space where sign language can live and thrive first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Sign language interpreters at rap concerts go viral for a reason. There’s something genuinely arresting about watching BSL in full flight: the expressiveness, the grammar operating in three-dimensional space, a face carrying as much meaning as the hands. People who’ve never encountered it before tend to stop scrolling. And then the clip ends, and the Deaf community goes back to navigating a world that wasn’t built with them in mind.

Deaf culture has arguably never had more mainstream presence. Rose Ayling-Ellis won Strictly Come Dancing in 2021 and became one of the most recognized faces on British television; CODA took home the Best Picture Oscar in 2022; the British Sign Language Act received royal assent that same year, legally recognizing BSL as a language of England, Scotland, and Wales for the first time. And yet across the entire United Kingdom, with 18 million people living with some degree of hearing loss, there is not a single dedicated cultural center built for and by the Deaf community. Not a permanent one.

Urban planner and activist Amanprit Arnold has been sitting with this for years. Now she’s doing something about it.

Arnold was born deaf and received cochlear implants at 21. Her design agency, Disability Urbanism, advises city planners and developers on accessibility. But the DeafCity Hub campaign is different. The goal is to create a building designed from the ground up around DeafSpace principles, a set of architectural guidelines developed specifically for Deaf users, and to make it a national gathering point for Deaf arts, culture, and community life. “There is greater visibility of deaf people in the media,” Arnold has said, “but when it comes to property and place-making for them, there’s nothing. We have a really strong cultural identity element and we need somewhere to celebrate that, somewhere made for us.”

Why the built environment speaks hearing by default

To see why a dedicated center matters, it helps to know what sign language asks of the spaces it inhabits. BSL is not, as Arnold puts it, “just spoken word translated into hands.” It’s a spatial language with a three-dimensional grammar, where expression and mouth movement carry meaning alongside the hands. Corridors need to be wide enough that two people can walk and sign at the same time without dropping the thread. Lighting needs to be natural and soft to reduce eye strain during long exchanges. Glass and mirrors get placed to extend sightlines. Seating goes in circles or arcs so groups can see everyone’s hands and faces at once. These aren’t luxury features. They’re the basic conditions for a conversation.

Most buildings offer none of this, and the effect is more significant than hearing people tend to assume. A narrow corridor puts signers in single file and stops the conversation. A poorly lit room makes faces unreadable. A standard rectangular boardroom table angles signers away from each other in ways that become genuinely exhausting over time. Even the acoustic design of an ordinary coffee shop, which most hearing people never consciously register, can make conversation hard for someone relying on both residual hearing and lip-reading together. When Arnold meets people for coffee, she sits outside, not because she prefers it but because the inside wasn’t built for how she talks. “Nowhere in London is specifically designed for me,” she has said.

The London College of Fashion’s East Bank campus is one of the few public buildings in the UK designed to full DeafSpace standards, and visitors tend to notice something they struggle to name: an ease, a sense of the building not fighting them. That’s what Arnold is trying to create.

Reviving a dream that never quite died

This isn’t the first time someone has tried. In 1986, during a particularly energized period in Deaf history, plans were drawn up for an International Deaf Cultural Centre in London: a theater, an exhibition space, a Deaf history archive, a bar, a quiet room, a hostel. Arnold has the original blueprints. They never turned into anything, but she has kept returning to them over the years. The 1980s were a charged time for Deaf communities on both sides of the Atlantic. In the United States, civil rights protests were building; Marlee Matlin became the first deaf actor to win an Oscar for Children of a Lesser God in 1986; Gallaudet University, founded specifically for Deaf students, appointed its first deaf president. In the UK, the BBC launched See Hear, and subtitle provision began to improve, though the road to legal recognition moved slowly. The British Sign Language Act didn’t pass until 2022, and a GCSE in BSL isn’t expected until 2028.

In September 2026, DeafCity Hub secured what’s called a “meanwhile” space, a building sitting unused while it awaits redevelopment, through a partnership with Westminster City Council and the Oxford Street Development Corporation. Arnold has a year to demonstrate what a dedicated Deaf cultural center could look like in practice. The space won’t meet full DeafSpace standards, and it won’t be permanent, but she’s treating it as an incubator, a way to build the evidence base and attract a developer partner for something that lasts. “We need to design and shape accessibility and inclusivity from the start,” she has said. “A meanwhile space won’t be perfect, but it will act as an incubator to develop this idea further.”

She also wants to address a frustration most Deaf people know well: that accessing mainstream cultural events generally means planning your schedule around a single interpreter-supported performance per production, usually offered on a weekday afternoon. “Theatres and cinemas will have an accessibility page on their websites, but performances with interpreters are rare,” Arnold has noted. “You have to go to one specific show, and that’s normally set for noon on a Tuesday when most of us are at work.”

Deaf Gain and the question of what gets preserved

There’s a question running beneath all of this that has nothing to do with architecture: what happens to a culture when medicine increasingly has the power to change who belongs to it? Cochlear implants have transformed life for many people with hearing loss, and their adoption has contributed to a significant decline in deaf schools across the UK, from 75 in the early 1980s to 22 now. Arnold has an implant herself and attended a deaf school as a teenager, an experience she describes as genuinely formative. She isn’t against the technology, but she’s noticed that the cultural dimension tends to disappear when the medical conversation takes over; the question of what cochlear implants do to a community rarely gets asked alongside the question of what they do for an individual.

The concept she comes back to is “Deaf Gain”: the idea that deafness isn’t a deficit to be corrected but a perspective that brings something genuinely different into the world. Arnold’s father was race relations director for Birmingham City Council in the 1990s, and her grandfather was a trade unionist and antiracism campaigner. She mentions this with a certain ease, as if the family pattern is self-explanatory enough that it barely needs saying. The longer-term vision for DeafCity Hub is an international network of hubs, each built to DeafSpace standards, each Deaf-owned and Deaf-led. “Most communities have their own spaces,” Arnold has pointed out. “I think creating DeafCity Hub as a deaf-owned and deaf-led arts space would assert that our culture is also rich.”

There’s a quote that circulates among Deaf activists, tracing back to the founding of Gallaudet University: “We travel the world to learn about cultures and people. We go into their country to visit them. We now have a country.” Arnold keeps a copy of the 1986 blueprints. She has a year in a meanwhile space and a case she’s been building for longer than that. Whether the funding follows is a different question. The argument, at least, is hard to argue with.

articles.personality_title: DeafCity Hub aims to build the UK’s first cultural center designed for the Deaf community
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Although British Sign Language (BSL) has gained legal recognition and Deaf culture is more visible in media, the UK lacks a dedicated cultural center designed for Deaf people. Existing buildings rarely meet the special needs of sign language users, making everyday communication difficult.

**What happened** – Amanprit Arnold, a Deaf urban planner and activist, started the DeafCity Hub campaign to create a building designed around DeafSpace principles. These guidelines shape spaces to support sign language, such as wide corridors for signing side-by-side and natural lighting to help read facial expressions. In September 2026, Arnold secured a temporary “meanwhile” space in London to show what a Deaf cultural center could be like.

**Impact** – This project is important because it addresses how most places are built for hearing people, often making communication exhausting or impossible for Deaf users. DeafCity Hub will offer a space where Deaf culture can be celebrated, arts can be shared, and community life can thrive. It also highlights the idea of “Deaf Gain,” which sees deafness as a unique culture and perspective, not a problem to fix.

**What’s next step** – Over the coming year, Arnold will use the temporary space to develop ideas and prove the need for a permanent Deaf cultural center. This will help attract partners and funding to build lasting DeafCity Hubs across the UK and potentially internationally, all led by Deaf people and designed with their needs in mind.

**One-sentence takeaway** – DeafCity Hub is creating a new kind of cultural center that truly supports Deaf language and community, filling a long-standing gap in the UK.
articles.personality_title_fr: DeafCity Hub veut créer le premier centre culturel dédié aux sourds au Royaume-Uni
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Bien que la Langue des Signes Britannique (BSL) soit désormais reconnue légalement et que la culture sourde soit plus visible dans les médias, le Royaume-Uni ne dispose d’aucun centre culturel spécialement conçu pour les personnes sourdes. La plupart des bâtiments existants ne répondent pas aux besoins particuliers des utilisateurs de la langue des signes, rendant la communication quotidienne difficile.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Amanprit Arnold, urbaniste et militante sourde, a lancé la campagne DeafCity Hub pour créer un bâtiment conçu selon les principes DeafSpace. Ces règles architecturales favorisent des espaces adaptés à la langue des signes, comme des couloirs larges pour signer côte à côte et un éclairage naturel pour mieux lire les expressions faciales. En septembre 2026, Arnold a obtenu un espace temporaire à Londres pour montrer ce que pourrait être un centre culturel sourd.

**Impact** – Ce projet est important car il répond au fait que la plupart des lieux sont conçus pour les entendants, rendant la communication épuisante voire impossible pour les sourds. DeafCity Hub offrira un espace où la culture sourde pourra être célébrée, les arts partagés, et la vie communautaire renforcée. Il met aussi en avant le concept de « Deaf Gain », qui considère la surdité comme une culture et une perspective uniques, et non comme un problème à résoudre.

**Prochaine étape** – Durant l’année à venir, Arnold utilisera cet espace temporaire pour développer ses idées et démontrer le besoin d’un centre culturel sourd permanent. Cela aidera à attirer des partenaires et des financements pour construire des DeafCity Hubs durables au Royaume-Uni, et peut-être à l’international, tous dirigés par des sourds et conçus selon leurs besoins.

**Résumé en une phrase** – DeafCity Hub crée un nouveau type de centre culturel qui soutient réellement la langue et la communauté sourdes, comblant un vide de longue date au Royaume-Uni.
articles.personality_title_es: DeafCity Hub busca crear el primer centro cultural diseñado para la comunidad sorda en el Reino Unido
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Aunque la Lengua de Señas Británica (BSL) ha sido reconocida legalmente y la cultura sorda es más visible en los medios, el Reino Unido no tiene un centro cultural dedicado diseñado para personas sordas. La mayoría de los edificios no cumplen con las necesidades especiales de quienes usan la lengua de señas, dificultando la comunicación diaria.

articles.title: One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
articles.summary: “Your mind follows the thread, one by one, row by row. You know? It’s like meditation. I don’t like machines.”
articles.content:
Weo, a prisoner at the Central Women’s Correctional Institution in Bangkok, prefers to sew by hand. She tried the sewing machine, but noticed that her mind was calmer when threading with her fingers directly. By not using a machine, she can produce a unique pattern that is hard to find in conventional shops.

She is explaining this to a group of design students who, sketchbooks in hand, are walking through the rows, observing the women who sew.

As time passes, some lose their initial apprehension and sit across from them, picking up fabric samples. Others ask about the products they are making. Some borrow their needles and, with the women’s guidance, try a bit of sewing themselves. A few sit on the floor in the basket-weaving corner with the women who have, by now, mastered the skill.

Today, the students have left the classroom behind to spend their morning at Thailand’s first women’s prison, where approximately 150 women learn weaving, knitting and machine sewing to make marketable products.

The students’ task is to design a product that these women can manufacture during their sentences.

© UNODC/Laura Gil

Through the wall

The initiative, launched in November 2025 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the Thailand Institute of Justice (TIJ) pairs design students with incarcerated women to create modern, sustainable products that can be sold outside prison.

Earlier this year, 22 students visited the prison and interacted with the women who are now manufacturing new products. Their designs had to appeal to modern consumers, be practical and tell a story linked to rehabilitation that would raise awareness of the critical role vocational training plays in reducing recidivism.

“The stigma surrounding those who have made mistakes has long been a wall in our society. To help them cross that barrier, we must restore their human dignity,” said TIJ’s Chontit Chuenurah.

“By weaving their stories into these products, we use the creativity of the youth to build a bridge between the prison and the outside world, replacing fear with understanding.”

Under the theme Through the Wall, the initiative seeks to dismantle physical and social barriers, helping incarcerated women return successfully to society, she added.

“The project aims to create prison-made goods that appeal to modern consumers while equipping correctional officers with essential marketing skills,” said Aki Okanan, former prison reform expert at UNODC.

The project also raises international awareness of the role of rehabilitation and vocational training in reducing re-offending she added.

Time well spent

A panel of judges evaluated nine projects from 19 students in a competition earlier this year.

The winner was Time-Made, featuring intricately smocked watch straps.

For the students behind the design, time has a two-fold meaning: the sentence that prisoners can reduce by working in prison, and the time that people outside value, a privilege sometimes taken for granted.

“We wanted our product to remind people that we can use time carefully and meaningfully. That we can watch our time,” says Game, 21, co-winner of the competition.

© UNODC/Laura Gil

First steps

All designs received support for product development and marketing, and the winning product, together with a selection of others, will be produced in collaboration with partner correctional facilities.

Natty, also 21, has been studying lifestyle products for three years. She had expected the prison to look gloomy and scary and was surprised to find the workroom bright and airy. Still, she noticed that most prisoners used dark colours.

“I want to take the skills they have and show them brighter fabrics and see what happens,” she said.

Sitting by Weo’s side, Ana*, from Latin America, tells the story of how she was caught attempting to smuggle cocaine into Bangkok. After four years in prison, she can produce perfect stuffed animals and is fluent in Thai, although she has never seen Thailand outside prison.

“I heard it’s beautiful here, but it doesn’t matter. After this, when I manage to get back to Brazil, I will start an import business and sell stuffed animals from Thailand. I know how to do it. I have the connections, and I speak the language.”

As the students pass through the gates and security controls to leave, their enthusiasm wanes. Although the prisoners cannot leave, this collaboration connects them to the outside world, the first step in reintegration.

*Name changed to protect identity.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.personality_title: Design students and incarcerated women in Thailand create products that break prison stigma
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Thailand, about 150 women in a women’s prison learn skills like sewing, weaving, and knitting. These skills help them make products while serving their sentences. Usually, people outside prison don’t understand or trust those who have been jailed.

**What happened** – In November 2025, a project started that brings design students from outside the prison to work with the incarcerated women. The students visit the prison, watch the women work, and then design new products that the women can make and sell. The project is called Through the Wall and is run by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime and the Thailand Institute of Justice.

**Impact** – This project helps change how society sees people in prison by showing their creativity and skills. The products are designed to attract buyers outside prison, helping women earn money and feel valued. It also teaches prison officers marketing skills. For example, one winning design was watch straps made with careful hand stitching, symbolizing the value of time for prisoners and people outside.

**What's next step** – The winning designs and other products will be developed and sold with help from partner prisons. This will give women more opportunities to practice their skills and prepare for life after prison. The project also aims to raise awareness worldwide about how training and work can reduce the chance of people going back to prison.

**One-sentence takeaway** – In Thailand, a creative partnership between design students and incarcerated women is helping break down prison stigma through meaningful work and new products.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des étudiantes en design et des femmes détenues en Thaïlande créent des produits pour briser la stigmatisation carcérale
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Thaïlande, environ 150 femmes dans une prison pour femmes apprennent des compétences comme la couture, le tissage et le tricot. Ces compétences leur permettent de fabriquer des produits pendant leur peine. Habituellement, les personnes à l’extérieur ne comprennent pas ou ne font pas confiance aux personnes incarcérées.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En novembre 2025, un projet a été lancé pour mettre en relation des étudiantes en design avec des femmes détenues. Les étudiantes visitent la prison, observent le travail des femmes, puis conçoivent de nouveaux produits que les femmes peuvent fabriquer et vendre. Ce projet s’appelle Through the Wall et est organisé par le Bureau des Nations Unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC) et l’Institut thaïlandais de la justice.

**Impact** – Ce projet aide à changer la façon dont la société voit les personnes en prison en montrant leur créativité et leurs compétences. Les produits sont conçus pour attirer des acheteurs à l’extérieur, aidant les femmes à gagner de l’argent et à se sentir valorisées. Il enseigne aussi aux agents pénitentiaires des compétences en marketing. Par exemple, un design gagnant était des bracelets de montre cousus à la main, symbolisant la valeur du temps pour les détenues et les personnes à l’extérieur.

**Prochaine étape** – Les designs gagnants et d’autres produits seront développés et vendus avec l’aide de prisons partenaires. Cela offrira aux femmes plus d’opportunités de pratiquer leurs compétences et de se préparer à la vie après la prison. Le projet vise aussi à sensibiliser le monde entier à l’importance de la formation et du travail pour réduire la récidive.

**Résumé en une phrase** – En Thaïlande, un partenariat créatif entre étudiantes en design et femmes détenues aide à briser la stigmatisation carcérale grâce à un travail utile et de nouveaux produits.
articles.personality_title_es: Estudiantes de diseño y mujeres encarceladas en Tailandia crean productos que rompen el estigma de la prisión
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Tailandia, unas 150 mujeres en una prisión femenina aprenden habilidades como coser, tejer y hacer punto. Estas habilidades les permiten fabricar productos mientras cumplen su condena. Por lo general, las personas fuera de la prisión no entienden ni confían en quienes han estado encarcelados.

**Qué pasó** – En noviembre de 2025, comenzó un proyecto que une a estudiantes de diseño con mujeres encarceladas. Las estudiantes visitan la prisión, observan el trabajo de las mujeres y luego diseñan nuevos productos que las mujeres pueden fabricar y vender. El proyecto se llama Through the Wall y está dirigido por la Oficina de las Naciones Unidas contra la Droga y el Delito y el Instituto de Justicia de Tailandia.

**Impacto** – Este proyecto ayuda a cambiar cómo la sociedad ve a las personas en prisión mostrando su creatividad y habilidades. Los productos están diseñados para atraer compradores fuera de la prisión, ayudando a las mujeres a ganar dinero y sentirse valoradas. También enseña a los oficiales de prisión habilidades de mercadeo. Por ejemplo, un diseño ganador fueron correas de reloj hechas a mano, que simbolizan el valor del tiempo para las presas y para las personas fuera.

**Próximo paso** – Los diseños ganadores y otros productos serán desarrollados y vendidos con la ayuda de prisiones asociadas. Esto dará a las mujeres más oportunidades para practicar sus habilidades y prepararse para la vida después de la prisión. El proyecto también busca crear conciencia mundial sobre cómo el entrenamiento y el trabajo pueden reducir la reincidencia.

**Frase clave** – En Tailandia, una colaboración creativa entre estudiantes de diseño y mujeres encarceladas está ayudando a romper el estigma de la prisión a través de un trabajo significativo y nuevos productos.

articles.title: Too young to run, old enough to protest: West Africa’s unfinished democratic bargain
articles.summary: Young people are old enough to vote and old enough to protest but are often told they need experience before they can hold political office.
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In 2018, young Nigerians won a fight that had taken years to organise. The Not Too Young To Run campaign helped push through a constitutional amendment lowering the age limits for several elective offices. Eight years on, the legal victory has not made politics much easier for them. Party nomination and expression-of-interest forms can cost as much as 100 million naira (USD 75,000). Earlier this year, one Nigerian state set the nomination fee for a local government chairmanship at NGN 30 million (USD 22,000), reportedly more than the office’s official earnings over a full four-year term.

At the legal ceiling, election campaign spending is now at an all-time high in Nigeria. In February 2026, President Bola Tinubu signed the Electoral Act 2026 into law, doubling the presidential spending limit from NGN 5 billion to 10 billion (about USD 7.5 million) and raising the governorship limit from NGN 1 billion to 3 billion (USD 2.2 million). These are no small numbers for a young candidate.

That gap between being allowed to run and being able to run hung over a conference room in Dakar from September 8 to 10. Convened by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) Commission and Legis360, the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference brought delegates from 12 countries together to discuss the barriers to young people’s political participation in the region.

Nelson Asusiya, a young parliamentarian from Ghana, described a generation told to wait its turn while being used as poster children for political parties and civic movements, and rarely given actual power.

Yet, the people being asked to wait are the majority. Young people make up about 70 percent of the region’s population, according to the conference communiqué.

Barriers to youth participation in West African politics

Across West Africa, young people remain largely absent from decision-making bodies despite their demographic weight. Political parties remain important gatekeepers, controlling who gets nominated, how candidates are selected and, in many cases, whose networks and resources can carry them through an election.

The Not Too Young To Run campaign in Nigeria showed what organised pressure can achieve. But it also exposed that changing the rules is not the same as changing who can afford to use them.

Cynthia Mbamalu, director of programmes at Yiaga Africa, which led the campaign, told the conference that while the amendment lowered the legal barrier, the political space remained more open on paper than in practice, with young aspirants still facing structural and financial barriers to contesting and winning.

Ezenwa Nwagwu, a Nigerian civil society leader, called the result a contradiction: Young people are old enough to vote and old enough to protest, but are often told they need experience before they can hold political office. He also rejected the idea that young Africans are impatient and drifting from democracy. Democracy, he argued, is measured not by its “dividends” of roads, hospitals and jobs, but by the freedom to question power.

Protests in West Africa

Across West Africa, protest has long been one of the ways citizens challenge political power. In 2012, Senegal’s Y’en a Marre movement mobilised young people against poor governance and President Abdoulaye Wade’s bid for a third term. In Burkina Faso, Le Balai Citoyen (“The Citizen’s Broom”) drew on young urban citizens to oppose Blaise Compaoré’s attempt to change presidential term limits. These movements showed how street politics could turn constitutional questions into issues people could see and feel in everyday life.

But protest has also met repression and contributed to distrust in formal institutions, as the #EndSARS protests in Nigeria showed.

An estimated 577 protests took place across West Africa in 2020 alone, according to a 2025 study of social movements in Africa. The frequency of such mobilisation points to a region where citizens, particularly young people, are repeatedly demanding a greater say in how they are governed.

But the region’s political institutions are themselves under strain. On January 29, 2025, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formally withdrew from ECOWAS, the regional bloc that convened the Dakar conference. The three countries, all under military rule, had formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and established a confederation in 2024, deepening a political rupture that has reshaped West Africa’s regional order.

For young West Africans, the withdrawal means millions of young people in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger now live outside the regional bloc that convened the Dakar conference. Yet many of the questions discussed there: political participation, democratic governance and youth inclusion, remain relevant to them.

Speaking with Global Voices in Dakar, Babatunde Afolabi, director of political affairs at the ECOWAS Commission, said negotiations with the Sahel states are progressing cautiously. He said:

One of the benchmarks for measuring progress is the ability of the parties to engage. We’ve already started on that trajectory. It’s still early days.

He said a July summit in Freetown, Sierra Leone, called for the talks to expand to peace and security, because “we’re still the same people. Although the AES countries have left, we have a lot in common.”

But the most concrete measure he offered was a year away.

“One year from now,” Afolabi said, he wants the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON), the conference’s main outcome, established, operating and partnered with ECOWAS. “That would be a good measure of progress,” he said.

Nigeria’s campaigners proved in 2018 that young people can rewrite the rules. The harder test, in Dakar and far beyond it, is whether anyone will rewrite the price.

For now, getting through the door can cost as much as NGN 100 million (USD 75,000).

articles.personality_title_es: Los jóvenes de África Occidental obtienen el derecho a postularse pero enfrentan nuevos retos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En África Occidental, los jóvenes representan alrededor del 70 % de la población. Tienen derecho a votar y protestar, pero a menudo enfrentan límites para ocupar cargos políticos. Muchos creen que necesitan más experiencia antes de postularse.

**Qué pasó** – En 2018, una campaña llamada Not Too Young To Run logró bajar la edad mínima para postularse a cargos políticos en Nigeria. Fue un gran avance para los jóvenes que quieren ser líderes. En septiembre de 2026, una conferencia en Dakar reunió a líderes jóvenes de 12 países para hablar sobre los obstáculos que aún enfrentan en la política.

**Impacto** – Aunque la ley cambió, los candidatos jóvenes aún enfrentan grandes problemas. Postularse puede costar decenas de miles de dólares, lo que es demasiado caro para muchos. Los partidos políticos controlan quién puede postularse, y los jóvenes a menudo carecen de recursos y redes. La conferencia mostró que, aunque tienen derechos legales, las oportunidades reales para ganar siguen siendo limitadas.

**Próximo paso** – La conferencia llevó a planes para crear la Red de Observadores Juveniles de África Occidental (WAYON). Este grupo trabajará con la organización regional ECOWAS para ayudar a los jóvenes a participar más en política. También hay negociaciones con países que salieron de ECOWAS para mejorar la paz, la seguridad e incluir más voces jóvenes.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los jóvenes de África Occidental ganaron el derecho legal a postularse, pero los altos costos y las barreras políticas aún dificultan su plena participación en la democracia.
